THE LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION (DR. MANMOHAN SINGH): 
Madam Chairperson, as this Session comes to an end, we can look back with a 
reasonable sense of satisfaction that two important Constitution Amendment Bills 
were passed and that this House and the other House made history when three Bills, 
creating three new States, were also passed with the cooperation of all the sections of 
the House. Mrs. Gandhi always laid emphasis that the role of the Congress party will 
be that of a responsible and constructive Opposition. To the best of our ability, we 
have tried to play that role as well as we can. I thank the hon. Leader of the House for 
the cooperation that we have received from him and the hon. Minister for 
Parliamentary Affairs. I think their joint efforts contributed a great deal to the smooth 
functioning of this House. Madam, we thank the hon. Chairman, you and the 
Secretary-General and his staff. We owe a special debt of gratitude for all the guidance 
that we have received from the Chairman and your goodself, Madam. 
Of course, we have some disappointments. But I do understand the reasons being 
beyond our control. The fact that the Women's Reservation Bill is still not on the anvil 
is a matter of disappointment to us. But I draw  satisfaction from the fact that when this 
matter was raised in the House, the hon. Prime Minister gave a categorical assurance 
that the Government would try to evolve a consensus, but if that consensus could not 
be evolved, the Government would nevertheless come forward with the Bill for 
consideration of Parliament. Madam, we were keen that before the Prime Minister 
went on his foreign tour, there ought to have been an exhaustive discussion on foreign 
policy. It is a matter of disappointment that though this discussion was also scheduled, 
for no fault of the Government, it could not take place. 
There are also other important discussions which we wanted. For example, on the 
National Agriculture Policy, our farmers are facing considerable difficulties. The 
National Agriculture Policy sets out a visi on. But we need a concrete programme of 
action to give shape to that vision. And it would have been a great advantage if the 
House had an opportunity to discuss the National Agriculture Policy. We are also very 
keen—we are now in the third year of the Ninth Five Year Plan-that the Ninth Five 
Year Plan, after a long delay, should come up for discussion in this House. This has 
not been possible. But I am not blaming the Government. I do understand that there are 
reasons why some of these things could not be taken up.

OBITUARY REFERENCES 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Hon. Members, this House wishes to place 
on record itS condolences at the passing away of Shrimati Sirimavo 
Bandaranaike, former Prime Mi nister of Sri Lanka, on 10 th October. 
2000. 
Sh'imati Bandaranaike has left an indelible mark on our times 
and hers was a pioneering roie in the politics of democratic change. 
She made a unique contribution to the progress of non-alignment and 
co-operation among developing countries. The people and the 
leadership of this country will cherish the memory of her friendship. 
We deeply mourn the loss of Shrimati Bandaranaike. 
Hon Members, I also refer with profound sorrow to the 
passing away of Shri Sitaram Kesri, former Member; Shri C. 
Subramaniam, a former Union Minister and a Member of the 
Constituent Assembly; and Prof. Shantilal Kothari, a former Member of 
this House 
Shri Sitaram Kesri passed away after a brief illness on the 
24th October, 2000, at the age of 81. Born at Danapor, Patna, in 
November, 1919, Shri Kesri had his education at Rashtriya Vidyalaya 
1 

RAJYA SABHA [20 November, 2000]  
of Bihar, Danapore and Bihar Vidyapith. An active social and political worker, 
Shri Kesri plunged into the freedom struggle at an early age and took an 
active part in the Quit India Movement  of 1942. He was imprisoned several 
times during the freedom movement. Shri Kesri was associated with various 
social welfare organisations and devot ed his entire life for the welfare and 
uplift of the downtrodden, the weaker and trie vulnerable sections of the 
society. 
Shri Kesri had a very long and distinguished Parliamentary career. 
He was a Member of the Fourth Lok Sabha and represented the State of Bihar 
in this House from July, 1971 to April, 1974; April, 1974 to April, 1980; July, 
1980 to July, 1986; April, 1988 to Apr il, 1994; and April, 1994 to April, 2000. 
Shri Kesri served as a Union Minister for several years and held the portfolios 
of Parliamentary Affairs, Shipping and Transport and Welfare. Shri Kesri was 
President of the Indian National Cong ress from September, 1996 to March, 
1998 and was elected unanimously as Leader of the Congress Parliamentary 
Party on January 3, 1997, Sober, mild-mannered, soft-spoken and kind-
hearted, Shri Kesri endeared himself to one and all. 
In the passing away of Shri Kesr i, the country has lost a noted 
Gandhian, a veteran freedom fighter and an eminent Parliamentarian. 
Shri C. Subramaniam, popularly known as CS, a former Union 
Minister and a Member of the Constituent Assembly, passed away on 7 th 
November, 2000 at the age of 90. 
Born at Pollachi . in Tamil Nadu in January, 1910, Shri Subramaniam 
had his education at Madras. A lawyer by  profession, Shri Subramaniam took 
an active part in the freedom struggle right from his student days and was 
imprisoned during the Quit' India 
Movement. 
Shri Subramaniam was Chairman, Committee on the Aeronautics 
Industry during 1967-69; National Commission on Agriculture during 1970-
1971; and UN Panel on Nutrition. He wa s also-a Member of the Governing 
Council of the International Wheat 
2 

[20 November, 2G00j        RAJYA SABHA 
and Maize Improvement Centre, Mexico; and Board of Governors of 
the International Rice Research Institute, Manila, 
Shri Subramaniam had a very long, distinguished and 
illustrious legislative career. He was a Member of both the Constituent 
Assem'bly and the Provisional Parliament. Later he became a Member 
of Madras Legislative Assembly and was Minister of Finance, 
Education and Law in the Government of Madras during 1952-1962. He 
was also a Member of the Third, Fifth and Sixth Lok Sabhas. Shri 
Subramaniam also served as a Union Minister for several years and 
handled important portfolios like Steel, Mines and Heavy Engineering, 
Food and Agriculture, Community Development and Co-operation, 
Planning Industry and Science and Technology, Finance and Defence, 
and was also Deputy Chairman, Planning Commission. He also 
adorned the august office of Governor of Maharashtra during 1990-93. 
Shri Subramaniam played a key role in heralding the Green 
Revolution in India. For his dedicated services, the nation bestowed 
on him its highest award, the "Bharat Ratna", in 1998- He was also 
author of several books in Tamil and English. 
In the passing away of Shri C. Subramaniam, the country has 
lost a true Gandhian, an able administrator, a Statesman and a 
visionary. 
Prof. Shantiiai Kothari passed away on the 14" November, 
2000 at the age of 76. Born in October, 1924 at Sirohi, Rajasthan, 
Prof, Kothari had his education at Beawar in Rajasthan; Wilson 
College, Bombay; University of California and University of London. 
A teacher by profession, Prof. Kothari was associated with the 
freedom struggle right from his student days, and took part in the Quit 
India Movement and was imprisoned several times. Prof, Kothari 
served as Senior Lecturer, M.S. University, Baroda; Reader, Munich 
Univetsity, Germany; and Director, Re search Programme in Political 
SvJh2>/iojr Project. 
3 

RAJYA SABHA [20 November, 2000] 
Prof. Kothari was awarded the Mary Keating Dass Foundation 
Prize by Columbia University in 1953 for his book "India's Emerging 
Foreign Policies" and also had several other publications to his credit. 
Prof. Kothari represented the State of Rajasthan in this House 
from April, 1964 to April, 1970. 
In the passing away of Prof. Kothari, the country has lost a 
noted freedom fighter and an academician of distinction. 
We deeeply mourn the passing away of Shri Sitaram Kesri, 
Shri C. Subramaniam and Prof. Shantilal Kothari.

RE. LAW AND ORDER PROBLEM IN DELHI 
THE LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION (DR. MANMOHAN SINGH): Mr. 
Chairman, Sir, a serious law and order situation has been created in the capital city 
of Delhi. The violent protests of workers and owners of those affected by the 
Supreme Court decision for relocation of polluting industries have left the city 
burning. Law and order in the capital city is the direct responsibility of the Central 
Government. Therefore, Sir, we demand that the hon. Home Minister should make 
a statement on this subject. 
Sir, we are all for respecting the decisions of the Supreme Court, but Sir, 
the problem that we are dealing with is a problem which has a large human 
dimension. We all want that the environment should be protected, safeguarded. 
The essential life support systems of the capital city need to be preserved and 
protected, but we cannot be oblivious to the fact that all this must be done, taking 
into account the interests of the workers and others affected by the processes of 
environment protection. We cannot preserve and protect the environment by 
perpetuating the poverty and sufferings of the downtrodden. It is in this context that 
the Government of the National Capital Territory of Delhi has been asking the 
Central Government to make suitable amendments to the Master Plan so that this 
whole problem can be looked at from a wider human angle, taking into account 
both the environmental aspect and interests of the affected workers who need 
assistance for rehabilitation, for alternat ive piece of land. We cannot take a 
mechanic view of all this. Therefore, Sir, I demand that the Government should 
make, without any loss of time, a statement on this subject. 
SHRI NILOTPAL BASU (West Bengal): Sir, we have been watching that 
on this issue, several Ministers have been making statements outside, in the Press, 
but it has a very complex dimension, as the Leader of the Opposition has rightly 
pointed out. This issue has been lingering on for the last five years; and, 
particularly, from this side, we have, time and again, raised our concern about the 
livelihood of the workers. Now, the total number of people affected, including 
their families, is to the tune of fifty lakhs. I think, we cannot remain a silent 
spectator to all that is happening. So, the Government should come forward to 
make a statement and take everybody into confidence

THE MINISTER OF COMMUNICATIONS (SHRI RAM VILAS 
PASWAN): (a) and (b) A statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
Yes, Sir. A paragraph titled "Package of concessions to existing Cellular 
and Basic Telephone Service Operators" has been included in the Report of 
Comptroller and Auditor General of India for the Year ended March, 1999 
(No. 6 of 2000). 
Government does not agree with the observations made by Comptroller 
and Auditor General of India. The Government considers that the policy 
regarding migration of the existing licensees to the New Telecom Policy, 1999 
(NTP-99) regime of revenue sharing arrangement was formulated as a result 
of informed and institutionalized decision in best public interest making 
pragmatic adjustments warranted by ground realities in relation to the Telecom 
Industry. The uniform application of NTP-99 which was desirable to provide 
a level playing field to all operators, was also aimed at ensuring accelerated 
growth of telecom sector by bringing in multipoly, better accessibility and 
improved / cost effective service to customers and this midcourse correction

policy.

 SHRI K. RAMA MOHANA RAO:

Statement 
(a) and (b) Yes, Sir. A Committee comprising representatives of Indian

Resource Management in the Public Sector Banks. This Committee in its

Poverty Alleviation Programme in Andhra Pradesh 
*21. SHRI K. KALAVENKATA RAO: Will the Minister of FINANCE be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether the World Bank has ranked Andhra Pradesh among the 
poorest States; 
(b) if so, the authentic figures about the number of families living below the 
poverty line in Andhra pradesh; 
(c) the State Government's contention in regard to the number of families 
below poverty line; and 
(d) the action taken to implement poverty alleviation programme and 
reduce poverty in Andhra Pradesh? 
THE MINISTER OF FINANCE (SHRI YASHWANT SINHA): (a) 
Though World bank does not rank States in India in relation to poverty, it has, in 
its Report entitled 'INDIA: Reducing Poverty, Accelerating Development' 
published in 2000, used real per capita income statistics to place major Indian 
States in high, middle and low income category on the basis of their relative 
position. According to per capita income criterion, Andhra Pradesh with tenth 
rank has been included in 'middle income group'. 
(b) The number of persons living below me poverty line in Andhra 
Pradesh was 153.97 lakhs (22.19% of the State's total population) in 1993-94 as 
per estimates based on the 50th Round of National Sample Survey. 
(c) The State Government did not agree to poverty being estimated on die 
basis of the expenditure pattern as reflected in the findings of me Survey. Instead it 
felt that the estimates of poverty needed to be made by eliminating 
26 

[21 November, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
the impact of the price depressing effect of the food subsidy scheme, funded 
from the State Exchequer. At a later stage, the State Government also wanted 
adoption of an earlier method of poverty estimation, known as the Task Force 
Method, to be used for estimating poverty. 
(d) Ninth Plan has adopted a three-pronged action plan to reduce poverty 
in the country i.e. accel eration of economic growth, human and social 
development and direct attack on poverty in all the States of India, including 
Andhra Pradesh. 
Measures to boost indigenous oil production 
*25. SHRI R.P. GOENKA: Will the Minister of PETROLEUM AND 
NATURAL GAS be pleased to state: 
(a) the steps being taken to increase the supply of oil from indigenous 
sources in view of the high international oil prices; 
(b) what is expected to be the supply of oil from indigenous sources in 
the next three years; and 
(c) how much of the indigenous production will be in the private sector? 
THE MINISTER OF PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS (SHRI RAM 
NAIK): (a) Government has taken several steps to increase crude oil production 
in the country which include:—  
(i) To improve the recovery factor from existing major fields by 
implementing Enhanced Oil recovery (EOR)/Improved Oil Recovery 
(IOR) schemes. These would also help in accelerating oil production 
from the fields. 
(ii)   To add reserves by exploring in the deeper layers in the producing 
areas. 
(iii)   To explore in die new areas specially in deep water and difficult 
frontier areas. 
(iv)   To develop faster the newly discovered oil fields. 
(v)   To increase workover and stimulation operations. 
(vi)   to increase exploration efforts through the New Exploration 
Licensing Policy (NELP) 
(vii)   To increase use of 3-D seismic surveys in new and producing areas. 
27 

RAJYA SABHA [21 November, 2000] 
ONGC has also taken steps by way of advancing their plans and inputs 
to produce additional 0.5 Million Metric Tonne (MMT) of crude oil over and 
above the annual Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) target of 24.6 MMT 
in the current year. 
(b) and (c) The indigenous oil production during the year 2001-02 is 
estimated to be about 32.30 MMT, incl uding the estimated crude production 
of 3.85 MMT from the current producing fields of private/joint venture 
companies. The production for the subsequent 2-3 years would have been of a 
similar magnitude; however, measures enumerated above are expected to 
increase the production.

Non-Payment of Money-orders 
*35. SHRI NANA DESHMUKH: Will the Minister of 
COMMUNICATIONS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that non-payment of money-orders to addresses 
at distant places is a matter of the day which causes inconvenience to the 
remitter also; 
41 

RAJYA SABHA [21 November, 2000] 
(b) whether it is also fact that on the reporting of such cases to the 
Press these are paid on duplicate money-orders; 
(c) if so, the number of such cases detected during the last one year; 
and 
(d) the penal action taken against the guilty officers? 
THE MINISTER OF COMMUNICATIONS (SHRI RAM VILAS 
PASWAN): (a) to (d) It is not a fact that non-payment of money orders to 
addresses at distant place is a regular occurrence. Generally money orders are 
paid on time to the payee irrespective of where he is residing as per 
departmental norms for delivery. Modernization of money order service 
through the use of VSAT network is improving its efficiency. Non-payment 
of money orders cause inconvenience to the remitter as also to the payee and 
the Department is alert in dealing with such complaints, in addition to regular 
administrative steps for monitoring/transmission/payment of money orders. 
Such monitoring includes verification of paid money orders selectively by 
supervisory officials. As soon as a complaint is r eceived, it is acknowledged, 
indexed and an enquiry letter is issued to the paying office. There is a long 
standing provision in the de partmental rules that in case no reply is received 
within 10 days from the paying office, a duplicate money order is got issued 
and paid. The Department receives comp laints through various sources like 
Ministers Office, Secretary (P)'s Office, MPs/VIPs, PMO, President Secretariat 
and Directorate of Public Grievances and also directly from individual 
remitters. Complaints received through th e press are only 0.2% of the total 
complaints. Prompt and effective action is taken on all such complaints. During 
the year 1999-2000, the Department handled a total number of 11.37 crores of 
money orders and a total of 56,840 complaints about non-payment of money 
orders were received including the complaints appearing in the press. If any 
official is found responsible for deficien t service, he is suitably punished as 
per provisions of relevant rules. During the year 1999-2000, a total of 663 
officials were imposed different kinds of punishments in the country for 
complaints against postal services including those relating to money orders.

141. SHRI B.J. PANDA: Will the Minister of COMMUNICATIONS be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have a proposal to expand the mobile internet; 
(b) if so, the steps taken in that regard during the last three years; 
(c) the plan drawn up for expansion of Mobile Internet Network till the 
end of Ninth Five Year Plan; and 
(d) the details of various efforts made for the expansion of Mobile 
Internet in the country? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF 
COMMUNICATIONS (SHRI TAPAN SIKDAR): (a) to (d) The New Telecom 
Policy-99 (NTP) envisages that Cellular Mobile Service Providers (CMSPs) 
shall be free to provide, in its service area of operation, all types of mobile 
services including voice and non-voice messages, data services and PCOs 
utilizing any type of network equipment, including circuit and/or packet 
switches, that meet the relevant International Telecommunication Union (ITU)/

As per the information gathered from Cellular Operators Association of 
India, "The Internet on Mobile Telephony has been made possible by 
introducing Wireless Application Protocol (WAP)". Some of Cellular Operators 
in India have recently started WAP se rvices and other are planning to 
progressivly introduce it. Expansion of Mobile Internet will depend on Market 
demand. There is no common plan for the whole cellular industry. Each 
operator is implementing after assessing business potential in their area of 
operation. It is very difficult to forecas t any kind of growth etc. as it is in 
infancy stage even in the rest of the world. Mobile Internet access is being 
provided by individual operators based on business potential as it involves 
additional investments. Competition rs driving the plans. 
The Ninth Five Year Plan of Department of Telecom is for expansion of 
cellular mobile and internet services and not specifically for mobile internet. 
VSNL has enabled its internet service to be usable by mobile users. 
VSNL has also provided "Webcell" Servies based on WAP. Using a WAP 
phone any mobile subscriber can acces s VSNL website, read mail and surf 
the web.

Review of SEBI code regarding hostile take-overs 
154. SHRI R.P. GOENKA: Will the Minister of FINANCE be pleased 
to state: 
(a) whether the present provisions in SEBI regulations favour hostile 
take-overs by allowing the raider to acquire upto IS per cent of the equity 
before open offer; 
(b) whether SEBI has any proposal of reviewing the take-over code; 
and 
(c) whether the exercise of voting rights by FIs and FIIs in a take-over 
bid create management uncertainty? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRI 
BALASAHEB VIKHE PATIL): 
(a) The SEBI (Substantial Acquis ition of Shares and Takeovers) 
Regulations, 1997 do not differentiate between a hostile and friendly takeover. 
Any acquirer who holds less than IS per cent of voting capital is allowed to 
91 

RAJYA SABHA [21 November, 2000] 
acquire up to 14.99 per cent without triggering an open offer. When an acquirer 
desires to cross IS per cent they can do so after making a public offer in 
terms of the takeover regulations. Any acquire who crosses 5 per cent of 
voting capital of the target company is however, required to disclose his 
shareholding to the target company, which in turn is required to inform the 
stock exchanges under the regulations. 
(b) SEBI has reconstituted a committee under the Chairmanship of 
Justice Bhagwati, in June 1998, to review the SEBI (Substantial Acquisition 
of Shares and Takeovers) Regulations, 1997. 
(c) The exercise of voting rights by financial institutions and foreign 
institutional investors is their prerogative.

Impact of price rise in Petro-Products on Economy 
165. SHRI NANA DESHMUKH: Will the Minister of FINANCE 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that increase in the domestic price of petro-
products would hit growth and make inflation go up; 
(b) if so, what has been its overall impact on the economy especially 
industrial and agricultural growth; 
98 

[21 November, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
(c) whether it is also a fact that on the external account higher exports 
particularly of software combined with the decline in non-oil imports would offset 
the adverse impact of a higher oil import bill current account deficit of about one 
per cent of GDP; and 
(d) if so, what are the actual figures on this account? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRI 
BALASAHEB VIKHE PATIL): (a) and (b) Sharp increase in crude oil prices from 
$ 11 per barrel in January 1999 to over $ 33per barrel in November 2000, is 
bound to have implications for domestic energy costs, thus pushing up not only 
the domestic costs of production, but even generating inflationary expectations due 
to rise in prices of LPG,  kerosene, petrol, ATF etc. which are used for final 
consumption. 
In the estimates of the latest available inflation rate at 7.27% three fourth 
of the price rise is accounted for by the rise in fuel-electricity sector prices as a 
consequence of the high crude oil prices. 
(c) and (d) During the first half of the current financial year, imports of 
petroleum crude and products have increased sharply by 86.2% (in Dollar terms) 
due mainly to continued hardening of international crude oil prices. However, 
adverse impact of such surge imports have been contained by a strong 
performance on the export front (by 22%) and a mild contraction in Non-POL 
imports (by 1.8%) thus resulting in a marginal improvement of trade deficit 
during April-September, 2000. 
Software service export during 1999-2000 grew by 5.3% to US $ 4015 
million on top of the increase of 49% in 1998-99. The growth rate witnessed in 
recent past is expected to be sustained during 2000-01 
The current account deficit in 1999-2000 was only 0.9% of GDP. The 
sharp rise in POL imports during 2000-01 will, other things remaining the same, 
widen the current account deficit significantly. But the buoyancy in exports of 
goods and software service exports combined with the slow growth in non-oil 
imports will help to moderate the current account deficit to a level which will be 
well manageable.

increase in intenational oil prices in 1999-2000. The performance of the 
economy in the face of all these adverse developments has been 
commendable and reflects the resillience that it has acquired. The trends in 
the economy are closely monitored and under constant

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PETROLEUM AND 
NATURAL GAS (SHRI E. PONNUSWAMY): (a) and (b)The Members of Parliament 
have been enquiring from time to time about the justification of inclusion of different 
locations in the LPG Marketing Plans and also giving suggestions for inclusion of 
certain new locations in the Marketing Plans in order to meet the requirements of the

As per the existing policy, the following criteria are adopted for setting up 
economically viable LPG distributorship in different parts of the country: 
(i) All urban locations with a population of 10,000 and above by including

population of 10,000 and above. 
(iv) Villages within 15 Kms. radius around towns having population of 1 
lakh and above. 
Only those locations which satisfy the above criteria are included in the 
Marketing Plan.

Recommendations of Water Asia Conference 
238. SHRI NANA DE SHMUKH: Will the Minister of WATER 
RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Water Asia 2000 Conference and Exhibition 
with latest technologies and services was held in New Delhi during September, 
2000; 
(b) whether it is also a fact that th e Conference had made fruitful and 
final recommendations for creating awareness and interest in general public 
particularly about waste water management and water conservation; and 
(c) if so, what are the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRIMATI BIJOYA CHAKRAVARTY): (a) to (c) Yes Sir. 
The Water Asia 2000 Conference and Exhibition with latest technologies and 
services was held in New Delhi between 18th September, 2000 to 20th 
September, 2000. The conference also ma de the following fruitful and final 
recommendations relating to Waste Water Management and Water 
Conservation:— 
1. There is a need for integrat ed water management through 
conservation and use of waste wate r recycling, artificial recharge 
of aquifer and rain water harvesting. Ground Water recharge, roof 
water harvesting may be incorporated in the building bye laws and 
incentive may be given to house owners to provide such facilities. 
2. In the planning of urban extensions, the availability of water, 
arrangements for collection, transportation and treatment of waste 
water and drainage needs to precede development. 
157 

RAJYA SABHA [21 November, 2000] 
3. There is an urgent need for adopting waste water reclamation and 
reuse practices which are technically sound, financially viable, eco-
friendly and sustainable in the lo ng run so as to reduce pollution 
load in the receiving water bodies and have water fit for use by the 
population residing in the downstream reaches. 
4. Industrial waste water in no case be allowed to discharge into water 
bodies without appropriate/adeq uate treatment conforming to 
Pollution Control Board norms. 
5. There is an urgent need to strengthen Rural as well as Urban Water 
Supply and Sanitation system by sustainable available coverage, 
quantity and quality-wise. This w ill involve people's participation 
and ensuring operation and maintenance of facilities.

* 16. PROF. M.M. AGARWAL: Will the Minister of COMMERCE AND 
INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have chalked out any scheme for the 
development of industrially backward districts in the country; 
(b) if so, the details thereof along with the names of industrially backward 
districts of the country; 
(c) if not, the specific reasons therefor; and 
(d) the steps being taken or proposed to be taken by Government under the 
liberalisation policy in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE AND 
INDUSTRY (DR. RAMAN): (a) and (b) Yes Sir. Several Centrally Sponsored 
Schemes are in operation for the development of backward areas in the country in the 
form of Infrastructure Development Schemes, Subsidy Schemes and New Industrial 
Policy Package for the North Eastern Region. 
Besides, Ministry of Finance, Department of Revenue has declared 123 
industrially backward districts in the country for granting concessions under the 
Income Tax Act, 1961 to industrial units set up in these districts. 
176 

[21 November, 2000: RAJYA SABHA 
State-wise list of these districts classified as category 'A' & 'B' given in the 
statement (See below) 
The details of these Schemes and incentives are give below:— 
Infrastructure Development Schemes 
(i) Growth Centre Scheme: Brought into operation in 1991, it 
envisages development of 71 Growth Centres in selected backward 
areas throughout the country which would be endowed with basic 
infrastructure facilities like power, water, telecom, etc. to enable 
the States to attract industries. 68 Growth Centres have been 
sanctioned and are under development. 
(ii) Integrated Infrastructure Development Scheme: Announced in 
1991 and implemented by the Ministry of Small Scale Industries 
and Agro and Rural Industries, the Scheme envisages development 
of infrastructure facilities for small industries to facilitate location 
of industries in rural/backward areas. 
Subsidy Schemes: 
(i) Transport Subsidy Scheme: Introduced in July, 1971 and recently 
extended upto 2007, this scheme is to promote industries in hilly, 
remote and inaccessible areas. Subsidy ranging from 50% to 90% 
is admissible under this Scheme on transport costs incurred on 
movement of raw materials and finished goods from the designated 
railheads/ports upto the location of the industrial units. 
(ii) Industrial Policy Package for North East: In view of its peculiar 
geographical conditions and continued backwardness, a new 
Industrial Policy and other concessions were announced for the 
North Eastern Region in December, 1997 which, besides the 
Growth Centre Scheme, HD Schemes, Transport Subsidy Scheme 
as well as Excise and Income Tax Exemptions for a period of 10 
years, has the following Subsid y Schemes exclusively for this 
region: 
(a) Central Capital Investment Subsidy Scheme: —It provides for 
subsidy @ 15% of the investment in plant and machinery subject 
to a maximum of Rs. 30 lakh to industrial units to be set up in 
identified locations. 
(b) Central Interest Subsidy Scheme: It provides for subsidy @ 3% 
177 

RAJYA SABHA [21 November, 2000] 
on the working capital loan to the industrial units. It was notified 
in February, 1999 and is valid upto 31.3.2007. 
(c) Central Comprehensive Insurance Scheme: It provides for 
reimbursement of insurance premium to the eligible industrial 
units. The scheme was notified on 14.7.99 and is valid upto 
13.7.2009. 
Tax Concessions: 
Under Section 80-IB of the Income Tax Act, industrial undertakings 
which begin operations after 1.10.1994 but before 31.3.2002 are entitled to a 
100% tax holiday for a period of five years in Category A industrially backward 
districts and three years tax holiday in Category B districts (refer Annexure). 
Such Industrial Undertakings in both categories of districts are entitled to a 
further deduction of 25% (30% in the case of companies) from their profits 
and gains for a period of another five years. 
Industrially backward States and Union Territories specified in Schedule 
Eight of the Income Tax Act, 1961, are also entitled to identical benefits for 
undertakings set up on or before 31.3.2002. 
(c) Does not arise. 
(d) Under die New Industrial Policy, 1991, the initiative for industrial 
development of backward areas lies primarily witii the State Governments. 
The Central Government supplements their efforts dirough various Schemes 
and incentives as detailed in reply to part (a) and (b) of the question.

Changes in Export Promotion Council membership norms 
18. SHRI R.S. GAVAI: Will the Minister of COMMERCE AND 
INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government proposes changes in Export Promotion Council 
membership norms; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) the reasons therefor; and 
(d) the measures proposed to strengthen EPCs? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE 
AND INDUSTRY (SHRI OMAR ABDULLAH): (a) to (d) The Committee 
constituted to look into the aspects of rationalization of election procedures of 
the Export Promotion Councils (EPCs) and the criteria to be adopted for 
restructuring of the EPCs so that they retain their relevance to the national 
export effort in the context of globlisation and economic liberalization, has 
made recommendations to streamline and strengthen the functioning of the 
EPCs. The Government has since accepted the recommendations of the 
Committee and issued model guidelines to all EPCs for adoption. Guidelines 
issued concerning membership norms of EPCs and measures proposed to 
streamline/strengthen EPCs are: 
1. Membership Norms : 
With a view to giving the voting rights and right of standing for election to 
various positions in the EPCs only to such members as are having an established 
standing over a minimum period of 3 years, it has been stipulated that there will 
be two categories of members namely: Associate Members and Ordinary 
Members. A person shall be eligible for admission to the Council as Associate 
Member on receiving the Import Export Code Number from Directorate General 
of Foreign Trade in respect of the product with which the Council is concerned. 
An associate member of the Council for atleast three continuous years would be 
eligible for ordinary membership of the Council provided the company represented 
by him has to its credit during the three financial years, immediately preceding, 
average exports in respect of the product of not less than Rs. 10 lakh for SSI and 
Rs.25 lakh for other than SSI companies. The ordinary member shall have the 
right to vote at the meetings of the Council and offer himself as a candidate at 
elections to various positions in the Council. 
205 

RAJYA SABHA [21 November, 2000] 
2. Greater attention to importan t existing and emerging industry 
segments: 
With a view to giving greater attention to some important segments 
within an existing industry group and also to provide coverage to commodities 
or sectors presently not covered by any of the EPCs, creation of a new vehicle 
viz. Export Promotion Forum (EPF) has been proposed. Permission for creation 
of an EPF may be considered on fulfilling the prescribed conditions. However, 
such permission shall be subject to: 
(a) The members agreeing to build up a corpus of Rs. 1.00 crore when 
the society is registered which should increase to Rs.3.00 crore 
within 4 years. The principle amount of the corpus shall be 
maintained intact and the EPF shall manage its expenses from the 
interest earnings, membership fees, etc. 
(b) The members of the EPF shall continue to be members of 
concerned EPC and shall continue to pay the membership fee to 
the concerned EPC till such time as the EPF is not converted into 
an EPC. (This will not be applicable to industry segments not 
covered under any EPC). 
(c) The staffing structure should be purely professional and as far as 
possible, the staff should be engaged on contract terms. The EPF 
shall meets its administrative expenses from its own resources. 
No funding shall be provided to them by the Government for this 
purpose. 
Subject to satisfactory performance on the basis of guidelines to be laid 
down by the Ministry of Commerce, the EPF will be eligible to be converted 
in a full-fledged EPC on completion of four years of its registration as an EPF. 
However, in the case of an EPC for industry segments not covered under any 
existing EPC, there will be no minimum waiting period. On conversion into 
an EPC, it shall be eligible for MDA grants for its export promotion activities 
only. It shall also be entitled to all other benefits/facilities available to the 
existing EPCs. 
3. Principles to be adopted by existing EPCs: 
Guidelines have been issued to the existing EPCs to engage the staff on 
contract terms as far as possible and to make the staffing structure purely 
professional over a period of five years. The existing EPCs have also been 
206 

[21 November, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
advised to build up a minimum corpus of Rs. 3 crore over a period of five 
years as applicable to the EPFs and to maintain the principal amount of the 
corpus intact and to manage its expenses from the interest earnings, 
membership fee, etc. 
4. Umbrella EPF for service industry: 
For important segments of Services Industry, an Umbrella EPF may be 
constituted. As and when individual service export industry builds up adequate 
demand and resources for a separate EPF, it may be allowed to break away 
from Umbrella EPF. 
5. Creation of a Service Cell: 
A Service Cell may be created in th e Ministry to provide focussed 
attention to the needs of service industries with an export potential. The Service 
Cell would also, inter-alia, advise regarding constitution of EPFs for individual 
service sectors. 
6. Election: 
It shall be the responsibility of the EPCs to ensure that the elections for 
the vacant seats are conducted well before the expiry of the term of the retiring 
members. The elected members shall automatically retire on the completion 
of their tenures. 
7. Voting Rights: 
Only elected members of the Managing Committee of EPCs shall have 
voting rights and the nominated/co-opted members shall not have such rights.

alcohol meant for potable purposes shall be under the total and exclusive control 
of the States in all respects, including the establishment of distillery, levy of excise 
duties and that all toner controls concerned with the manufacture of alcohol for 
exclusive supply to industries (other th an potable alcohol) shall be under the 
jurisdiction of the Central Government. By a subsequent judgement dated 11.3.97, 
a two Judge Bench of the Supreme Court in the case of Government of Haryana and 
others Vs. Haryana Brewery Limited and another [JT 1997 (10) SCC 665 = 
(1997) 5 SCC 758] has held that since the various decisions of the Hon'ble Court 
project different points of view, it is necessary fo formulate a coherent and 
effective formula so that the Union and the States should know their respective 
powers and jurisdiction and the matter should be placed before the Constitution 
Bench of the Supreme Court. The matter is presently before the Constitution Bench 
of the Supreme Court.

STATEMENT 
Salient features for establishment, maintenance and operation of Direct-to-
Home (DTH) Broadcasting service. 
(i) The applicant company shall be an Indian company, registered 
under the Indian Companies Act, 1956. 
(ii) The total Foreign Investment,* including FDI/NRI/OCB/FII in the 
DTH Broadcasting sector, shaU not be more than 49%, in which 
the share of FDI will not exceed 20%. 
Provided that the quantum represented by that proportion of the 
paid up equity share capital to the total issued equity capital of the 
Indian promoter Company held or controlled by foreign investors 
through FDI/NRI/OCB investments shall form part of the above 
said FDI limit of 20%. 
No Broadcasting Company and/ or Cable Network Company shall 
be eligible to own more than 20% of the total equity of an applicant 
Company at any time during the License period. 
Note: * Approvals for foreign equity shall be routed through the FIPB route. 
230 

[21 November, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
Provided further that the Licensee, at all times, shall keep the 
Licensor informed of any change in the holding pattern of the 
Equity. 
(iii) The applicant company must have Indian management control with 
majority representatives on the Board, as well as me CEO of the 
Company being a resident Indian citizen. 
(iv) There will be no restriction on the number of licensees and die 
license will be issued by the Government for a period of 10 years, on 
non-exclusive basis. 
(v) The applicant company shall be required to pay an entry fee of Rs. 
10 crores, in the beginning, In addition, 10% per year of the revenue 
collected by the platform owner from channels shall be payable to 
Government as annual fee. The licensee would also be required to 
execute a Bank guarantee of Rs. 40 crores valid fox the duration of 
the licence. Licensee will additionally be required to pay the license 
fee and royalty for spectrum used, as prescribed by the Wireless 
Planning Coordination authority (WPC), under the department of 
Telecommunications. 
(vi) The Licensing Authority shall ha ve the power, after recording the 
reasons in writing, to revoke/ suspend die license in public interest. 
However before taking such action the licensing authority will give 
the licensee an opportunity of being heard. The decision of the 
licensing authority shall be final. 
(vii) For violation of license condidons, in addition to any odier acdon 
which may include revocation of license, a penalty upto Rs. SO 
crores can be imposed by die Licenser on die Licensee. However, 
before taking such action the licensing authority will give die 
licensee an opportunity of being heard. The decision of die 
licensing audiority shall be final. 
(viii) The licensee shall establish the uplink Earth Station in India widiin 12 
mondis from die date of issue of licenses. All Content provided by the 
DTH platform to die subscribers, irrespective of its source, to pass 
dirough die common encryption and conditional access system, 
located within die Eaith Station, situated on Indian soil. 
(ix) The licensee shall ensure adherence to die Programme. Code (PC) and 
Advertisement Code (AC), laid down by the Ministry of 
231 

RAJYA SABHA [21 November, 2000] 
Information and Broadcasting, from time to time. Record of the 
programmes and advertisements carried on the platform to be kept 
by the Licensee for a period of 90 days after broadcast and to be 
made available to the authorised representative of the Licenser, as 
and when required. 
(x) The licensee shall provide access to various contents providers/ 
channels on a non-discriminatory basis. The licensee shall not carry 
any channels prohibited by the Ministry of I&B. 
(xi) Licensee shall provide access to the Licensing Authority or its duly 
authorised representative, to all its facilities including 
equipments, records, systems, etc. 
(xii) Though licensee can use the bandwidth capacity for DTH service on 
both Indian as well as foreign satellites, proposals envisaging use of 
Indian satellites will be extended preferential treatment. 
(xiii) The licensee shall ensure s ubscriber's interests through Single 
Conditional Access Technology, Single Subscriber Management 
System (SMS), an Open Architecture (Non-proprietary) Set Top Box, 
a Cast Iron Encryption System and an efficient, responsive and 
accurate billing and collection sy stem. The Licenser shall not use 
any equipment, which is identified as unlawful. 
(xiv) The Licenser reserves the right to prohibit the transmission or 
reception of programmes in the interest of national security or in the 
event of emergency/war or similar type of situation. 
Notwithstanding any agreement between the licensee and the 
content providers, the licensee shall stop forthwith, transmission of 
TV channels or any content, as and when directed to do so by the 
Licenser or any other designated lawful authority. 
(xv) The DTH facility shall not be used for other modes of 
communication, including voice, fax, data, communication 
Internet, etc. unless specific license for these value-added services has

(xvi) The licensee shall obtain cl earances/approvals, as may be

or from the Department of Space.

outside India.

World Development Report on Poverty Alleviation 
100. SHRI KARNENDU BHATTACHARJEE: Will the Minister of URBAN 
DEVELOPMENTAND POVERTY ALLEVIATION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the Worl d Bank in its recent study World 
Development Report 2000- 2001, Attacking Poverty has observed that growth and 
development alone are not enough to eradicate poverty; 
(b) whether it is also a fact that the Bank in the above mentioned study have 
made some specific suggestions to ensure poverty alleviation particularly in the 
developing countries; and 
(c) if so, the details thereof and the steps proposed to be taken to 
implement these measures? 
THE MINISTER OF URBAN DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY 
ALLEVIATION (SHRI JAGMOHAN): (a) Yes, Sir. The World Bank have recognized 
in its reports that poverty is more than inadequate income or human development it is 
also vulnerability and a lack of voice, power and representation. 
(b) and (c) Yes, Sir. The report has made some specific suggestions to ensure 
poverty alleviation, particularly in developing countries. However, there is no simple, 
universal blue print for implementing this proposed strategy. Developing countries need 
to prepare their own mix of policies to reduce poverty, reflecting national priorities 
and local realities. Choices will depend on the economic, socio-political, structural 
and cultural context of the individual countries—indeed, individual 
communities. While the report proposes a more comprehensive approach, priorities 
will have to be set in indivisual cases based on resources and what is institutionally 
feasible. The propose strategy identifies three ways to alleviate poverty:— 
(1) By promoting opportunity through  
(i) Encouraging effective private Investment,  
(ii) Expanding into international market, 
 (iii) Building the assets of poor people,  
(iv) Addressing asset inequalities across gender, ethnic, racial and 
social divides, 
 (v) Getting infrastructure and knowledge to poor areas — rural and 
urban. 
288 

[21 November, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
(2) By facilitating empowerment by making public action responsive 
to the needs of the poor people by way of 
(i) Laying the political and legal base for inclusive development, 
 (ii) Creating public administrations that foster growth and equity,  
(iii) Promoting inclusive decentralization and community development, 
 (iv) Promoting gender equity, 
(v) Tackling social barriers,  
(vi) Supporting poor people's social capital, 
(3) By enhancing security and reducing vulnerability an encourages 
investment in human capital and in higher return activities by way of 
(i) Formulating a modular approach to helping poor people manage risk, 
 (ii) Developing national programmes to prevent, prepare for an 
respond to macro shocks financial and natural,  
(iii) Designing national systems of social risk management that are 
also pro-poor,  
(iv) Addressing civil conflict, 
 (v) Tackling the HIV/AID epidemic.

DR. DASARI NARAYANA RAO (Andhra Pradesh): Mr. 
Chairman, Sir, I would like to draw the attention of the Government, 
through you, to the panic caused by spread of brain fever (Japanese 
Encephalitis) in epidemic form in Andhra Pradesh. 
These days, as many as 15 districts of my home State, 
Andhra Pradesh, are reeling under the panic of brain fever or 
Japanese Encephalitis, which has taken a heavy toll of human lives in

Chittoor, Prakasam, Guntur, Cuddapah, Nelbre, Krishna,

an epidemic.

THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF COAL 
(SHRI N. T. SHANMUGAM): Sir, I beg to move: 
"That the Bill to empower t he Central Government to 
direct the transfer of the land, or of the rights in or over 
land or of the right, title and interest in relation to a coal 
mine, coking coal mine or coke oven plant, vested in 
the Coal India Limited or in a subsidiary company to 
any subsidiary company of Coal India Limited or any 
other subsidiary company and to validate certain 
transfers of such tend or rights, be taken into 
consideration." 
Sir, the Central Government, .through nationalisation in 1972-

the right in the Coal India Limited. So far as the administrative 
purpose is concerned, the Coal India Limited created eight 
subsidiaries, namely, Bharat Coking Coal Limited, Western Coalfields 
Limited, Eastern Coalfields Limited, Central Mine Planning and Design 
Institute, Ranchi, South-Eastern- Coalfields Limited, Bilaspur, 
Northern Coalfields Limited, Singarauli, the Mahanadi  Coalfields 
Limited, Sambalpur and the Centra l Coalfield Limited Ranchi. They 
have transferred some land, for administrative purpose, to these 
subsidiaries. But there is some lacuna due to which they suffered 
some legal infirmities.  Therefore, now  this Bill is being moved to 
validate the transfers, with retrospective effect, that is, from the date 
of transfer. That is the main aim of the Bill.

subsidiary companies with the Coal India. Now they are not able to

rights. It can transfer the property to any party. In this way, a lot of 
litigation can be avoided. So, I welcome this Bill.

SHRI NT. SHANMUGAM: Mada m Deputy Chairperson, I 
have carefully listened to the debate on the Coal India (Regulation of 
Transfers and Validation) Bill, 1995 in the Hous e and also the points 
raised by hon. Members during the course of the debate. 
Hon. Member, Shri Bhatt, talked about the challenges of coal 
import and rationalisation of railway freight. Hon. Member, Shri 
Agarwal, spoke on the collection of stamp duty, the corruption in Coal 
India and the need for reorganisation of Coal India. Hon. Member, Shri 
Thirunavukkarasu, explained the provisions of the Bill and welcomed 
the Bill. Hon. Member, Shri Jibon Roy, felt that the Bill is legally not 
correct. 
He also mentioned that the present strike in Coal India Ltd. is 
due to this Bill. Hon. Member, Shri Margabandu, felt that the Bill would 
lead to privatisation. Shri Eduardo Faleiro talked about the coal mafia 
and issues relating to tribal land. Hon. Member, Shri S.S. Ahluwalia, 
talked about the history that led to the introduction of this Bill. He has 
also mentioned in detail about the latest coal-mimrtg technology, the 
linkage of coal with power production and issues realtihg to 
subsidiaries like ECL, BCCL, etc., and mine safety. Mine safety is 
governed by the Director-General of Mine Safety. There shall be no 
change in that position.  He has also mentioned 
319 

RAJYA   SABHA       [21 November, 2000] 
that mine safety should be taken up on a priority basis and that 
categorisation was not done properly. Hon. Member, Shri Gupta, said, 
"coal is black gold". He has also mentioned that the mines are not 
modernised and mine safety is ignored. He has mentioned about the 
underground fire also. He wanted a National Coal Policy to be 
formulated. 
The Bill has a restri cted purpose of  empowering the Central 
Government to direct the transfer of the land and its rights pertaining 
to all coal-mines or coke-oven plants vested in the Coal India Limited 
or.In a subsidiary company to any or other subsidiary company of 
Coal India Limited. This Bill is not in any way related to railway freight 
re-organisation of Coal India Ltd., import of coal, de-notification of 
tribal lands and transfer of land to multinationals, etc., nor is it a proxy 
for privatisation of coalmines. 
Now, I may point out that the absence of a formal legal title to 
the land, coke-oven plants, mining rights and other properties in the 
subsidiary companies of Coal India Limited has exposed them to 
litigation and other legal infirmities. This matte r was examined by the 
Committee on Public Undertakings. The Committee had directed that 
the transfer of rights in and over land and properties in favour of 
subsidiary companies, which are de facto managing the mines and 
properties vested in Coal India Limited, should be effected without any 
further delay. Two former Attorney Generals had also advised that this 
situation needs to be rectified through appropriate legislative 
measures. The Standing Committee on Industry also undertook a 
comprehensive examination of many of the issues raised during the 
discussion. The Report of the Standing Committee, which was laid on 
the Table of the Rajya Sabha on 27.7.2000, deals with these issues at 
length and, therefore, it may not be necessary for me to go into them 
again. The Committee had recommended adoption of this Bill. 
It has been pointed out that the same objective could have 
been achieved by effecting suitable amendments in the Coal Mines 
Nationalisation Act, 1973, instead of introducing this fresh Bill. It needs 
to be appreciated that lands, mining rights and other properties have 
been acquired by Coal India Limited through various Acts, that is, the 
Coking Coal Mines (Nationalisation) Act, 1972, the Coal Mines 
Nationalisation Act, 1973, the Coal Bearing Areas (.Acquisition and 
Development) Act, 1957 and the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, and 
through direct negotiations. An amendment to the Coal Mines 
(Nationalisation) Act would not have covered the lands and properties 
acquired through other statutes and modes. Hence, there is the need

RAJYA SABHA [22 November, 2000] 
(a) the details of the news-item published in the Lokmat Samachar 
on the 2nd October, 2000, under the caption, Vridhavastha Pension 
main vridhi hogi; 
(b) whether Government are considering any proposal to provide 
them other facilities also in addition to Vridhavastha pension; 
(c) if so, the details thereof; 
 
(d) whether Government are also considering the proposal to 
extend concessions to them in the inter- State buses and airlines like 
Air India; and 
(e) if so, the details thereof and if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF RURAL DEVELOPMENT (SHRI M. 
VENKAIAH NAIDU): (a) to (e) A Statement is laid on the Table of 
the House. 
Statement 
In his Address on the Senior Citizens Day at New Delhi on 1st 
October, 2000 (of which reports a ppeared in the Lokmat Samachar, 
Nagpur, Maharashtra and other newspapers), the Hon'ble Prime 
Minister had, inter alia, observed that while Government has been 
implementing the National Social Assistance Programme for the benefit 
of Senior Citizens who do not have access to economic sustenance and 
the National Old Age Pension Scheme is operated under this 
programme, the amount disbursed under the Scheme being modest, it is 
hoped that it would be possible to in crease the same with the help of 
State Governments. 
In addition to the pensions prov ided by the Central Government 
under the National Old Age Pension component of the National Social 
Assistance Programme, the Government in the Ministry of Rural 
Development have (in April, 2000) launched, the "Annapuma' Scheme 
under which foodgrains @ 10 kgs. per person are provided free of cost 
to aged destitutes, with an approximate coverage of 6.64 lakh persons. 
The care of old persons being primarily the concern of the Ministry of 
Social Justice And Empowerment, that Ministry are implementing An 
Integrated Programme For Older Persons wherein financial assistance 
upto 90% of the project cost is provided to NGOs for the establishment 
and maintenance of Old Age Homes, Day Care Centres and Mobile 
Medical Units as also non- institutional services for older persons. The 
Ministry have a Scheme of Assistance to Panchayati Raj 
Institutions/Voluntary Organisations/ Self-help Groups for the 
construction of Old Age Homes and Mobile Service Centres for older 
persons wherein grant of upto Rs. 30 lakhs is provided to eligible 
persons for, inter alia, the construction of Old Age Homes. 
12 

[22 November, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
The Ministry of Social Justice And Empowerment have indicated 
that they have recently drawn up a National Policy on Older Persons under 
which an Action Plan has been formulated (for the year 2000-2005) 
which is to be implemented in conjunction with various Ministries / 
Departments. As per this Action Plan, the Ministries of Surface Transport 
and Civil Aviation would consider:- 
(i) Fare concessions to senior citizens in Buses. 
(ii) Design buses to provide for easy entrance, exit and safety. 
(iii) Reservation of seats for older persons in Buses. 
(iv) Whether facilities could be provided to senior citizens to make 
air travel a comfortable experience and to lower the age of 
entitlement for air fare concessions for women. 
Amongst the other initiatives reported to have been taken by the 
Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment in pursuance of the National 
Policy on Older persons are:—  
(i) The National Council for Older Persons (NCOP) has been set 
up on 10th May, 1999 to operationalize the Policy. The first 
meeting of NCOP was held at New Delhi on 13th June, 2000. 
The members discussed the draft Action Plan for 
implementation of the National Policy on Older Persons. The 
process of finalisation of Action Plan is in progress. 
(ii) Aadhar has been set up to function as Secretariat of NCOP. It is 
being administered by Agewell Foundation, an NGO, with the 
financial assistance from the Ministry. The ma jor activities 
of Aadhar include receiving and taking follow up action on 
representations, the complaints and grievances of older 
persons. 
(iii) Both the ongoing Schemes of  the Ministry for Welfare of 
Older Persons have been reviewed and revised in the light of the 
National Policy. 
(iv) The Ministry commissioned a project called OASIS (an 
acronym for Old Age Social and Income Security) and 
appointed an 8 member Expert Committee, headed by Dr. S. 
A. Dave, former Chairman of UTI, to examine policy questions 
connected with old age income security in India and submit its 
recommendations to the Government. The Committee 
submitted its final report on 11.1.2000. 
13

expeditions disposal of Court Cases involving Older Persons. 
(vi) The Union Health Ministry has issued instructions to all the State 
Governments / UT Administrations for provision of separate queues 
for older persons at all stages. 
(vii) At the initiative and with the financial assistance of this Ministry, 
a Telephone Helpline for older Persons has been made functional 
from April, 1999 by an NGO called Agewell Foundation. 
(viii) The National Institute of Social Defence has started a six months 
course for home care of elderly disabled persons. This course will 
help to prepare a cadre of Geriatric Animators to render 
comprehensive care to the aged in their homes and in the 
community.

forces and modernization and upgradation of police and security forces with 
sophisticated weapons and communication system etc.

with regard to implementing effective border management. The concerned 
agencies of the two Governments remain in regular touch. There are also bilateral

Management and Home Secretary level talks.

enforcement agencies of both the countries and improved management of the

measures, including stepping up vigil along the contiguous border districts of 
India and Nepal, to counter activities inimical to India's interests.

was despatched by Ordnance Factory, Khamaria at Jabalpur to NAD 
Karanja on 1-12-1997 vide Railway Receipt No. D 111511 dated 1-12-
1997. The despatch details along with the Railway receipt was sent by 
Ordnance Factory, Khamaria to the consignee who was to monitor 
recept of the consignment. NAD, Ka ranja took up the issue of non-
receipt of the consignment with the Chief Commercial Superintendent, 
Central Railway, CST, Mumbai by letter dated 18-5-1998 endorsing 
copy to Ordnance Factory, Khamaria. On receipt of information, 
Ordnance Factory Khamaria also took up the matter with appropriate 
Railway authorities and detailed personnel to various probable stations 
en-route as also to stations as far as Mysore and Chennai where it

intimates the despatch details to the consignee to monitor the receipt of

effort is made both by consignee and consignor to trace the wagon. In 
addition necessary action through law and

Safety and security of common people 
293. PROF. M.M. AGARWAL: Will the Minister of HOME AFFAIRS be 
pleased to state: 
(a) the details of effective measures being taken by Government to provide 
adequate safety and security to the common people in the country; 
(b) whether it is a fact that Government have failed to provide adequate 
safety and security to the people of Bihar, Jammu and Kashmir, NER belt and 
other backward districts of the country; and 
(c) if so, the reasons therefor and Government's reaction thereto? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS 
(SHRI CHENNAMANENI VIDYA SAGAR RAO): (a) to (c) Despite some areas 
of concern, the law and order situation in the country is under control. The 
major concerns centre around Pak-sponsored terrorism in Jammu & Kashmir, 
inter-linked and externally supported subversive activities of militant groups 
in the North-East and the violence perpetrated by the Left Wing Extremist 
groups. "Public Order" and "Police" are State subjects and maintenance of law 
and order is the primary responsibility of the State Governments. It is for the 
State Governments to devise various methods and take concrete steps to improve 
the law and order situation in their States. The Central Government, however, 
keeps a close watch on various developments in the internal security scenario 
of the country and sensitises the concerned States in this regard. It also shares 
intelligence with the States from time to time. Central Para-Military Forces are 
also deployed whenever required by the States. Funds are also provided under 
various schemes to modernise and strenthen the State Police Forces.

consequence of proxy war unleased by Pakistan; and

it, minimise it or stop it? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME 
AFFAIRS (SHRI CHENNAMANENI VIDYA SAGAR RAO): (a) Having 
failed to occupy Jammu and Kashmir through conventional warfare, Pakistan 
is carrying out a low-intensity proxy war in Kashmir to bleed India. In J and 
K, die Pak agencies provide direct support to various terrorist groups in the 
form of training arming and financing them and in helping them to infiltrate 
into J and K. Along wim terrorist acts, die thrust is on subverise actions to 
destabilise and communa lise die situation, paralise economy and 
demoralise die State Administration. 
(b) To contain terrorism in Jammu and Kashmir, the Government has 
adopted a multi-pronged approach which includes, inter-alia, 
strengthening border management, neutralising plans of the terrorist by 
pro-active action against them in the hinterland, gearing up intelligence 
machinery, greater functional integration through and institutional frame 
work of operation Groups and Intelligence Groups of the UHQ at all levels, 
improved technology, weapons and equipments for security forces. 
Steps are being taken to flush out terrorist and curb militants activities 
including close vigil on border, establishment of more naka parties in depth 
or deeper, areas to check infiltration/exfiltration, more pickets, intensive 
patrolling and extensive cordon and search operations.

Statement 
Pending Border Disputes between Different States 
Maharashtra-Karnataka border dispute: 
Eversince the Reorganisaiton of states in 1956, there has been 
boundary dispute between Maharahstra and Karnataka, both 
demanding re-adjustment of boundaries on the basis of the language 
spoken by the people of their area. 
103 

RAJYA SABHA [22 November, 2000] 
Earlier efforts to resolve the dispute through mutual agreement having failed, 
theCbvemment of India appointed the Mahajan Commission in October, 1966. 
The Commission submitted its report on 2S.8.1967. Out of the total of 814 
villages claimed by State of Maharahstra, the Commission had recommended 
that 264 villages along with the towns of Nipani, Khanapur and Nandgad may 
be transferred from Karnataka to Maharashtra. The claim of Maharashtra to the 
town of Belgaum was rejected. Out of 260 villages claimed by Karnataka, the 
Commission recommended transfer of 227 villages to Karnataka from 
Maharashtra. While the Government  of Karnataka insisted on the 
implementation of the recommendations of die Mahajan Commission in toto, 
the Government of Maharashtra did not accept the recommendations. The 
dispute, therefore, continues to exist. 
Orissa-Andhra Pradesh border dispute: 
The boundary disputes between Orissa and Andhra pradesh relates to 63 
villages. Disputes relating to Kotiya group of 21 villages and Borramutha 
(total 22 villages) of Koraput district in Orissa dates back to 19SS and the 
dispute relating to rest 41 villages with Andhra Pradesh dates back to 1981-82. 
Punjab-Haryana-Himachal Pradesh border dispute: 
Consequent upon the reorganisation of the composite Punjab State in 
1966, the Central Government announced its decision on these disputes in 
1970. This included transfer of Chandigarh to Punjab and part of FazilkaTehsil 
of Punjab to Haryana etc. Three Commissions have been appointed so far to 
determine the specific Hindi speaking areas of Punjab which should go to 
Haryana in lieu of Chandigarh. 
Uttar Pradesh-Bihar and Uttar Pradesh-Haryana border dispute: 
The deep stream of river Ganga and Yamuna formed inter-State boundary 
between some parts of Uttar Prades h-Bihar and Haryana-Uttar Pradesh 
respectively. Due to frequent changes in the course of the river, the inter-state 
boundary keeps on fluctuating. Due to this disputes persist.

SHRI CO. POULOSE: 
Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to state: 
(a) the contribution of private sector in rural electrification in the

(b) whether Government are aware of th.; fact that the private 
distribution companies are extremely reluctant to continue with the 
power supply to the rural areas; and 
(c) if so, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER 
(SHRIMATI JAYAWANTI MEHTA): (a) Privatisation of electricity 
supply to the rural areas has been undertaken only in Orissa. In the State 
of Orissa where distribution companies have been privatized, the 
maintenance of rural electrification network is now under the

326.  SHRI V.V.RAGHAVAN: 
SHRI J. CHITHARANJAN: 
Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the sanction had been accorded to 
increase the installed capacity of the NTPC Thermal Plant at 
Kayamkulam by 1950 MW; and 
(b) if so, by when the construction will start? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER 
(SHRIMATI JAYAWANTI MEHTA): (a) and (b) Kayamkulam Combined 
Cycle Power Project (CCPP) Stage-II of 1950 MW (tentative) capacity 
is conceived as a regional project on regassified LNG as primary fuel.

oil prices resulting in corresponding increase in LNG prices, 
Kayamkulam CCPP Stage-II proposal would be firmed up only after 
availability of LNG at reasonable pr ices and terms and conditions of 
supply within a appropriate time-frame is confirmed.

Review of power scenario in the States  
327. SHRI B.J. PANDA: Will the Minister of POWER be pleased 
to state: 
(a) whether Government have reviewed the Power scenario in 
different states; 
(b) if so, when the last review was made; 
(c) the demand-supply position at present, State-wise; 
(d) whether Government have a proposal to bring about reforms 
in the power sector; and 
(e) if so, the details of the plan formulated in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER 
(SHRIMATI JAYAWANTI MEHTA): (a) and (b) AH Regional 
Electricity Boards hold regular monthly meetings to review State-wise 
current demand-supply position and to take corrective measures. The 
last such review in respect of Northern, Eastern, Western, Southern and 
North-Eastern Region was made on 8th November, 23rd October, 13th 
October, 7th November and 24th Oc tober, 2000 respectively. Minister 
of Power also held meetings with Power Ministers of Southern Region 
States on 10th July and with Power Ministers of Northern Region 
States on 20th October, 2000 to review the power scenario and other 
related issues in the States of these two regions. 
(c) State-wise Power Supply position  during October, 2000 and 
April-October, 2000 is given in the Statement (See below). 
(d) Yes, Sir. 
(e) A Conference of Chief Ministers/Power Ministers was held in 
New Delhi in February 2000. The co nference resolved that the key 
elements of the reforms strategy would be: 
(i)   Energy Audit at all level. 
(ii)   Time-bound programme of 100% metering of all 
consumers by December, 2001. 
(iii)   Reduction and finally elimination of power theft within 
a specified time-frame. 
(iv)   Strengthening/upgradation sub-transmission and 
distribution system by taking sub-station as an unit on a 
priority basis.

328. SHRI PARMESHWAR KUMAR AGARWALLA: Will the 
Minister of RURAL DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state:

schemes for implementation through the State Governments alongwith 
allocation of funds, State-wise;

followed for maintaining accountability; and

VENKAIAH NAIDU): (a) to (c) The Ministry of Rural Development 
implements the Jawahar Gram Samridhi Yojana (JGSY), the Employment 
Assurance Schemes (EAS), the Swarnjayanti Gram Swarozgar Yojana 
(SGSY), the Indira Awaas Yojana (IAY), the National Social Assistance

Ministry also Implements area development programmes, namely, 
Integrated Wastelands Development Progarmame (IWDP), Drought Prone 
Area Programme (DPAP) and Desert Development Progrmme (DDP) 
wherever applicable. A Statement showing the State-wise total 
allocation (Central and State) a nd utilisation of funds under these 
schemes during 1999-2000 is enclosed (See below). The utilisation of 
funds is continously monitored and release of the second instalment of 
funds is subject to utilisation of atleast 60% of the available funds. In 
addition, "graded cuts are imposed on the allocation to the States, if 
proposal for the second instalment is delayed.

Drinking water schemes in Andhra Pradesh 
338. DR. Y. LAKSHMI PRASAD: Will the Minister of 
RURAL DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) the schemes financed for improving drinking water facilities in 
the rural areas of Andhra Pradesh during the current financial year: and 
(b) the target for completion thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF RURAL DEVELOPMENT [PROF. 
(SHRIMATI) RITA VERMA]: (a) and (b) Rural Water Supply, being a 
State subject, is implemented by the State Governments under the State 
Sector Minimum Needs Programme (MNP). The Central Government 
supplements the efforts of the State Governments by providing financial 
assistance under the Central Sector A ccelerated Rural Water Supply 
Programme (ARWSP). The powers to plan, sanction and implement 
individual rural drinking water supply schemes have been delegated to 
the State Governments. As such, the details of schemes financed for 
improving drinking water facilities in the rural areas under the ARWSP are 
not maintained at the Central level. As per the Action Plan prepared by the 
Government of Andhra Pradesh, all the rural habitations of the State would 
be provided with safe drinking water facilities in five years, subject to 
availability of funds. 
However, sector reform projects have been sanctioned by the 
Government of India in respect of four pilot districts of Andhra Pradesh, 
namely, Chittoor, Khammam, Nalgonda and Prakasam with an 
objective of institutionalizing community participation in the Rural 
Water Supply Programme in the entire chosen districts. These projects 
have been prepared with a provisional project implementation schedule 
of three years. The sanctioned project costs in respect of these projects 
are as under:

(SHRI. DHANNAJAY KUMAR): (a) Expecting internaitonal 
competition in the textile sector following the changes in the world

compete internationally in the manufacture and export of clothing.

(b) The main objectives of the Policy are:—  
(i) Facilitate the Textile Industry to attain and sustain a pre-
eminent global standing in the manufacture and export of

(ii) Equip the Industry to withstand pressures of import 
penetration and maintain a dominant presence in the 
domestic market; 
(iii) Liberalise controls and regulations so that the different 
segments of the textile industry are enabled to perform in 
a greater 
competitive environment; 
(iv) Enable the industry to build world class state-of-the-art 
manufacturing capabilities in conformity with 
environmental standards, and for this purpose to 
encourage both Foreign Direct Investment as welt as 
research and development in the sector; 
(v) Develop a strong multi-fibre base with thrust of product 
upgradation and diversification; 
(vi) Sustain and strengthen the traditional .knowledge, skills 
and capabilities of our weavers and craftspeople; 
(viii Enrich human resource sk ills and capabilities with special 
emphasis on those working in the decentralised sectors 
of the Industry; and for this purpose to revitalise the 
Institutional structure; 
(viii) Expand productive employment by enabling the growth of 
the industry, with particular effort directed to enhancing 
the benefits tcthe North East region;

entire value chain of textile production and thereby 
facilitate the industry to achieve international standards

Entrepreneurs, Farmers and Non-Governmental 
Organisation in the fulfilment of these objectives.

• Maximising employment opportunities

Closure of textile mills can be  attributed to many factors 
including obsolete technology, increase  in cost of imputs, difficulties

(b) and (c) The policies of the Government are always aimed at 
development of the industry. However, due to complex, diverse and 
widely dispersed nature of the textile industry, it is but natural that at 
any point in time, some mills will be lying closed. However, the South 
East Asian crisis of 1997-99 and increasing competition due to 
globalisation process has added pressure on weak mills, leading to 
more closures in the last three years. 
The Government of India has enacted the Sick Industrial 
Companies (Special Provisions) Act, SICA, 1985 and established the 
Board of Industrial & Financial Reconstruction (BIFR) with a view to 
arranging the timely detection of sick & potentially sick companies and 
for the speedy determination of preventive, ameliorative and remedial 
measures which need to be taken in respect of such companies. The 
rehabilitation schemes sanctioned by BIFR include various measures 
like restructuring the capital, induction of fresh funds by the promoters, 
merger with the other companies, change of management, provision for 
working capital and term loans by banks and financial institutions. 
Further, Government has taken a number of steps to tackle the problems 
faced by textile industry and make it more competitive. Some of these 
are as follows:

the country, the government has launched the Technology

355. SHRI P. PRABHAKAR REDDY:  
SHRI J. CHITHARANJAN:  
SHRI  V.V. RAGHAVAN: 
Will the Minister of TEXTILES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government's New Textile Policy has since been 
announced; 
(b) if so, the highlights thereof; 
(c) whether Government are aware that there is large scale 
disappointment in the industrial and labour circles about the new textile 
policy; and 
(d) if so, steps proposed to be taken in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF TEXTILES 
(SHRI V. DHANANJAY KUMAR): (a) Yes Sir. 
(b) Broadly, the Policy proposes to:—  
(i)   Facilitate the Textile Industry to attain and sustain a pre-
eminent global standing in the manufacture and export of 
clothing; 
163 

RAJYA SABHA [22 November, 2000] 
(ii) Equip the Industry to withstand pressures of import penetration 
and maintain a dominant presence in the domestic market; 
(iii) Liberalise controls and regu lations so that the different 
segments of the textile industry are enabled to perform in 
a greater competitive environment; 
(iv) Enable the industry to build world class state-of-the-art 
manufacturing capabilities in conformity with 
environmental standards, and for this purpose to encourage 
both, Foreign Direct Investment as well as research and 
development in the sector; 
(v) Develop a strong multi-fibre base with thrust of product 
upgradation and diversification; 
(vi) Sustain and strengthen the traditional knowledge, skills and 
capabilities of our weavers and crafts people; 
(vii) Enrich human resource skills and capabilities, with special 
emphasis on those working in the decentralised sectors of 
the Industry; and for this purpose to revitalise the 
Institutional structure; 
(viii) Expand productive employment by enabling the growth of 
the industry, with particular effort directed to enhancing the 
benefits to the Norm-East region; 
(ix) Make Information Technology (IT), an integral part of the 
entire value chain of textile production and thereby 
facilitate the industry to achieve international standards in 
terms of quality, design and marketing;

of the State Governments, Financial Institutions, 
Entrepreneurs, Farmers and Non-Governmental Organisations 
in the fulfilment of these objectives.
