RAJYA   SABHA [24 November, 2000] 
CRF, has been released to the States as per the Scheme. The 
Central Teams were deputed to many flood affected States to 
assess the situation and I had also made aerial survey of the 
flood affected areas of the States of Arunachal Pradesh, Bihar, 
West Bengal and Andhra Pradesh. My Ministry coordinated the 
Central efforts with various C entral Ministries/Departments for 
providing relief to the affected people. Foodgrains at the BPL 
rates have been supplied to the State Governments particularly 
to the State of Bihar and West Bengal. Medicines, 
disinfectants, bleaching powder, halogen tablets, etc., were 
also sent to the affected States. 
As you may be aware, 75% of the annual rainfall is 
received during south-west monsoon period, from 1st June to 
30thSeptember, itself resulting in heavy rains and floods in 
many parts of the country, causing damage to life and property 
every year. The flood prone areas are Andhra Pradesh, 
Assam. Bihar, Himachal Pradesh, Karnataka, Madhya 
Pradesh, Punjab, Uttar Pradesh and West Bengal. The 
perennial States in regard to regular floods are Assam, North 
Bihar and Eastern parts of Uttar Pradesh. Central Water 
Commission in the Ministry of Water Resources is concerned 
with flood forecasting. India Meteorological Department 
provides necessary support th rough its Flood Meteorological 
Offices. They cater to the requirements of flood forecasting in 
different river catchment areas. FMOs provide Quantitative 
Precipitation Forecast in respect of catchment areas of 
important river to the CWC. Flood forecasting enables 
forewarning about impending flood, to what extent and for how 
long, so that necessary preparatory steps could be taken in 
time. The flood forecasting network consists of 157 stations 
situated in 11 States. 
Flood proofing measures help greatly in the mitigation 
of distress and provide immediate relief to the population in 
flood prone areas. It is essentially a combination of structural 
change and emergency action, not involving any evacuation. 
The techniques adopted consist of providing raised platforms 
for flood shelter for men and cattle and raising the public utility 
installation above flood levels. The progress achieved in flood 
control works as a result of various measures taken is that 
162,000 Km. length of embankments and 32,003 Km. length of 
drainage channel were constructed, 906 towns were protected 
and 4721 villages protected. 
Monitoring  of floods  is also done by remote sensing 
through satellites  which   is  one  of  the  effective  tools  to  
monitor  floods  and  assessment  of flood  damages  in  terms 
of area  inundated,  crop  area  submerged and villages 
marooned.

money from you. The Government of India is the giver. Why did 
you not create the Fund when you accepted in principle that the 
Fund has to be created as per the recommendation of the 
Finance Commission, to deal with a situation of natural 
calamities of a severe magnitude? The idea is that there should 
be a corpus of Rs.500 crores. First the Finance Ministry will 
give it from the Budget. Thereafter it will be recouped by

Minister is to create this Fund. After accepting the 
recommendations of the Finance Commission, why has this 
Fund not been created? What is the difficulty? Are they going 
to do that in the current session? 
The third aspect is that you have mentioned about 
some of the measures taken in regard to flood prevention and 
their success. Quite good, you have done something. But one 
of the major problems is about the information that you have 
given on the 17th of August. Mr. Minister, it is your Department.

have also quoted as per the information available from the 
Water Resources Ministry on the 26th l of September. But see 
how impractical you are. In the information that you gave on 
the 26th of September in regard to West Bengal, you are 
saying that the Ganges was flowing above the danger level but 
below the earlier record. Two other rivers, not the Ganges, 
created the whole flood in West Bengal. One is the 
Mayurakshi. and the other is the Damodar. There was an 
unprecedented rainfall in the catchments of the Mayurakshi 
and the Damodar from the 17th of September to the 26th of 
September. There is no reflection in the report of either in the 
Ministry of Agriculture. or in the Ministry of Water Resources 
that this unprecedented rainfall has created a situation where 
the floods are likely to occur. There are two reservoirs in the 
catchments of the Damodar and two in the catchments of the 
Mayurakshi, the Massanjar and the Tilpara. They were obliged 
to release the surplus water. Otherwise, it would have 
damaged the dam. If they release the surplus water, the down-
stream areas are bound to be inundated. Therefore, it is not 
relevant whether the Ganges is flowing above the danger level 
or not. When you visited those areas, surely, the people there 
would have briefed you about the relevant factor causing the 
flood by those two rivers. It is mainly because of the 
unprecedented rainfall in the catchments. 
Therefore, my submission to you is that, as you have 
mentioned, some medium-term and long-term measures are 
needed on this. You are fully aware of the fact that the 
Damodar embankments have not been fully completed. The 
project is incomplete because some other constructions have 
to be undertaken. That is not being done. So far as the 
Mayurakshi is concerned, it is one of the earliest project. The 
project was completed even before the First Plan started. It 
was a bilateral assistance programme from the Canadian 
Government; and the project was commissioned some time in 
1951. It did not have adequate flood control measures.

recurring feature. We create

PROF. M. SANKARALINGAM (Tamil Nadu): Sir, I fully 
support the sentiments expressed by the hon. Members in 
regard to the plight of people who are affected by the havoc 
caused by floods in various parts of the country. The people of 
West Bengal, Andhra Pradesh. Bihar, Madhya Pradesh and 
Kerala are the worst affected. Sir, this is an annual feature in 
our country. India is a vast country. If one-year floods affect the 
southern part, the next year it affects the western part, the third 
year it affects the eastern part and the fourth year it affects the 
northern part. So. at least, one part of the country is affected 
every year.  We ftave to save the people 
198 

[24 November, 2000] RAJYA   SABHA 
from this havoc caused by floods or drought. We are 
discussing the flood situation in various parts of the country. I 
really feel that West Bengal is the worst affected State. The 
statement of the hon. Minister itself reveals as to how much 
damage has been caused in West Bengal. We must extend our 
full support to the people of West Bengal and also to the 
people of other States who are affected by floods. Sir, this 
havoc caused by floods should be treated as a national 
calamity, not as a responsibility of the State. That is my view. I 
appeal fo the hon. Minister to treat this flood situation as a 
national calamity. Two years back, we experienced the same 
situation in Orissa. This year it has happened in West Bengal, 
Andhra Pradesh and other places. Some areas are affected 
mildly. Mostly the agriculturalists are affected. Their crops have 
got destroyed. The whole irrigation system has got disturbed. 
Tanks and channels have been disrupted. We have noted 
some breaches also. To set right all these things, it will take 
one or two years. The life of  agriculturists and people who are 
affected by floods becomes normal only after one or two years. 
It is very difficult to recoup the position. I would request the 
Central Government to study the matter in detail and establish 
a permanent Calamity Relief Commission. A group, consisting 
of experts, has to be appointed and they should go and visit the 
affected areas, After studying the problems, they should 
recommend some plans for redeeming the distress of the 
affected people. 
Sir, I wish to bring to the notice of the Government the 
situation prevailing in Tamil Nadu, though Tamil Nadu does not 
figure in the statement. It has been stated that Kerala has been 
affected. Sir, the southern-most part of Tamil Nadu borders with 
Kerala and, therefore, certain parts of Tamil Nadu, namely, 
Kanyakumari, Madurai, Ramnad and Tirunelveli districts are 
affected by the climatic changes in Kerala. The rainfall started 
on the 19 th of this month in al! these places, and it is still 
continuing. Big tanks have been breached; channels have been 
disrupted and the entire system of irrigation has been affected. 
So, I request the Government to consider this matter as a 
matter of national importance. The Eleventh Finance 
Commission has also recommended that the State 
Governments should be assisted by the Centre. It has also 
recommended that the Central Government should review the 
situation in the States. It has also specified the Centre-State 
ratio, saying that the Centre should bear 75 per cent of the 
damages and the State should bear the remaining 25 per cent.    
So. I request the Government to look into the matter and

the people who have been affected by floods.

SHRI R. MARGABANDU (Tamil Nadu): Mr. Vice-
Chairman, Sir, since independence, only one committee -- the 
one headed by Shri Kelkar 
200 

[24 November, 2000] RAJYA   SABHA 
-- had been constituted to find out the reasons as well as 
solutions, so far as floods in the Ganges were concerned. After 
that, no committee has been constituted for this purpose. Floods 
in India have become a regular phenomenon every year. One or 
the other part of the country is always affected by floods. Of 
course, Andhra Pradesh is affected very seriously. This year, the 
State of West Bengal has also been affected badly. Several parts 
of India have been affected. I do not want to level any charge 
against this Government. But Government after Government has 
not taken care to constitute any high-powered committee 
consisting of experts to examine the behaviour of the rivers and 
the reasons behind the floods. These have to be examined. 
Modern technologies are available. We have to have a scientific 
approach and a comprehensive plan to assess this situation. 
Whenever there are floods, which are shortlived, the Central 
Government gives assistance. But that is not sufficient. That 
assistance is only for a short period. If a family gets devastated 
by floods, it takes five to ten years to come back to normalcy, 
Sometimes, families are destroyed or ruined for ever. So, we 
have to evolve a long-term policy. This Government has to 
consider the constitution of a high-powered committee to find out 
the reasons as well as solutions to the problem of floods. After 
all, it is not difficult for the Government to identify the areas that 
are regularly affected by floods, as well as to devise measures 
that should be taken to control the fl oods. Only then, this 
problem can be solved. Calamities are taken very lightly and in 
a very casual manner. Whenever there are floods, people 
assess the situation through helicopters and so on and estimate 
the damages; and that's all. You have to solve the problem for 
all times to come. I do not think any long-term assistance has 
been given in this regard. I request the Government to lay a 
white paper on this issue. Also, we must have a foolproof flood 
management system and there s hould be a mechanism to 
control the floods. Many a time, floods are caused due to 
desiltation, deforestation and erosion of riverbanks. These are 
the main reasons for the floods. I would like to know whether the 
Government would come forward to save the life and property 
from the havoc caused by floods, especially in West Bengal, 
where the situation is alarming. So far as the State of West 
Bengal is concerned, there is also a report in which it is said that 
the Department of Education in the Ministry of Human Resource 
Development informed that it was not in a position to provide any 
assistance because that Ministry does not administer any 
scheme which provides for repair of school buildings that have 
been damaged due to excessive rains and floods. 
201 

RAJYA  SABHA   [24 November, 2000] 
On the one hand, the houses and school buildings have 
been devastated; on the other, the Ministry of Human 
Resource Development is saying that it has no scheme for 
them, and it would not help. What type of attitude is this? 
Should this type of an attitude be adopted by the Government? 
I, therefore, request the Government that all efforts should be 
made to help these people. The farmers and villagers are 
affected the most by these floods. As compared to rural areas, 
urban areas are not affected much by these floods. So, the 70 
per cent of our population which is residing in villages is 
affected by these floods. These poor people are rendered 
homeless, landless and their crops are devastated by floods. 
The Government should see to it that some effective steps are 
taken in order to save these people from floods. The 
Government should formulate a long-term project so that the 
people are saved from these natural calamities. 
[The Vice-Chairman (Shri Suresh Pachouri) in the Chair.]

SHRI H.K. JAVARE GOWDA (Karnataka): Thank you, 
Mr. Vice-Chairman, Sir. The unprecedented rainfall has caused 
a great havoc all over the country. As stated by the Minister of 
Agriculture, it is particularly severe in West Bengal. Andhra 
Pradesh, Karnataka and some other States. So far as 
Karnataka is concerned, these floods resulted in loss of 152 
human lives. Besides this, roads were damaged very badly; 
bridges were destroyed; public buildings and some 55.000 
houses were damaged; and cropped area in 56,000 hectares 
has also been damaged. The State Government of Karnataka 
has asked the Central Government for further financial 
assistance. But so far, the Government has not released the 
amount. The other important thing to be taken into account is 
the human feelings. At that time, whether it is the Central 
Government or the State Government, they had not anticipated 
that the loss would be of that magnitude and that it would 
cause so much havoc to human lives and property. I must also 
say that officers reach there in the normal course, that is, a 
long time after all this damage is done. What do they do? They 
say, "yes, you have suffered heavy losses, you have lost 
everything; but they do not talk about the relief or the 
compensation. Obviously, they would say ' we have written to 
the Government'. The State Government would say 'we have 
asked for financial assistance from the Central Government.' It 
is only after three or four months that some people would go 
there. Their coming after such a long period, does not serve 
any purpose. They cannot compensate the pain and agony

regard, is we should be prepared to meet such challenges.

management was primarily the responsibility of the State 
Governments.   He has very rightly said this.

the principal Opposition Party, also CPM's Dr. Biplab 
Dasgupta, who is. unfortunately, not here today, made was that 
the policy of this Government is a departure from the past. Sir, I

very opening submissions to the House. Very befittingiy and

great personalities of the past, principally, to late Pandit

Members' point that a nostalgia for the past, or, about great 
personalities of those times, or, the policies then adopted and 
of the state of the world then existing, is a suitable approach to 
meet the challenge of contempor aneity, particularly, when the 
world of today is characterised by change, the sheer velocity of

great inheritance that successive Governments have received,

what I had then said — in my opening remarks, i had said -- 
that we appfoach this responsibility of addressing the challenge 
of the present, rooted in the strengths of the past, with a vision 
of the future, about the true destiny of India. For, mind you, Sir, 
attaining that destiny is the ultimate national interest.

departure in India's West Asia policy; and this observation was

statements were issued on several days. But from the very

immediately issued its viewpoint clearly and

THE PROHIBITION OF SMOKING BILL. 2000 
SHRI KARTAR SINGH DUGGAL (Nominated):   
Madam, I move: 
That the Bill to provide for the prohibition of 
smoking of tobacco in any form in places of public 
work or use and in public service vehicles since 
smoking has been found injurious not only to the 
smokers but even more to the non-smokers and 
to make provision therefore and for other matters 
connected therewith, be taken into consideration. 
उपसभापितः ऐसा लगता है िक यह Ģावधान तो है क्यȗिक हवाई जहाज

SHRI KARTAR SINGH DUGGAL: Madam, smoking 
considered as a private problem until yesterday is a public 
hazard today. It has been proved beyond any doubt that 
tobacco smoking is injurious not only for the one who indulges 
in it, but it is also as much, harmful, if not more, for those 
around. Cosmetic measures like advertising "Smoking is 
injurious for health" etc. may have succeeded to an extent in 
the developed countries but    these    have    registered    little    
impact    in    the    developing    and 
259 

RAJYA   SABHA [24 November. 2000]  
underdeveloped countries. With the latest research revealing 
grave danger of passive smoking, it has become imperative to 
take stricter measures to curb this menace in our developing 
society in India. Hence this Bill about which the Government 
too, has already given an indication in reply to an Unstarred 
Question on December 10, 1999, that "the Government is 
examining the feasibility of formulating a comprehensive 
legislation for discouraging use of tobacco smoking." 
According to the Delhi Medical Association findings, 
recently reported in the Press, tobacco will emerge as a major 
killer by 2020.- It is estimated that nearly 3.5 million people 
annually die in the world from smoking-related diseases, of 
which two-thirds die in the developing countries. The World 
Health Organisation has reported that over 150 million children 
in the world die of tobacco-induced diseases, one-third of 
which, under five years, die due to acute respiratory infectious 
tobacco smoke. If the trend continues, tobacco use would kill 
nearly 10 million people every year. As it is, over 10 lakh 
people annually, or 3,000 every day, die on account of smoking 
in India. Several lakh more are disabled by tobacco-related 
diseases. The victims include those non-smokers who often 
remain in the company of smokers. 
The report goes on to say, "Tobacco contains harmful 
substances such as nicotine, carbon monoxide and lar. On 
inhalation, these substances enter the bloodstream affecting 
!he brain and causing heart and other ailments. Nicotine 
increases secretion of chemicals like adrenaline which 
increases the heart rate and blood pressure. Nicotine also 
interferes with the functioning of blood vessels, increasing the 
tendency of blood clots. Other adverse effects are respiratory 
infections, gastric ulcers, pregnancy complications, etc." 
Tobacco intake is a major contributing factor for 
causing cancer. It is reported that about 300 million would be 
afflicted by cancer in the next 25 years and about 200 million 
would die due to the disease. A WHO report says that tobacco 
use is responsible for 90 per cent of lung cancer and over 80 
per cent of chronic bronchitis cases. Also, 20 to 25 per cent of 
coronary heart diseases and stroke are attributed to smoking. 
Scientific data shows that there is unmistakable co-
relation between smoking and infertility. If a person smokes 
more than 20 cigarettes a day, his sperm count, a decisive 
factor in fertility, could drop by 60-70  per  cent.    The  infertility  
risk  is  not  confined  to men  alone.

chances of embryo implant. In pregnant women it can cause 
abortion, pre-term labour and dam age to the embryo.  It-could

SHRI KARTAR SINGH DUGGAL: Children are the 
main prey to tobacco smoking. Maladies in children include 
asthma, bronchitis, pneumonia, lung cancer and irritation to 
eyes, nose and respiratory tract. Presence of toxic component 
of tobacco smoke has been shown by scientists in the hair, 
body fluid and tissues of non-smokers exposed to smoking. 
According to WHO, about half of the world's children are 
exposed to tobacco smoke by the adults who smoke. For 
young children, major source of tobacco smoke is their parents 
and other household members. Maternal smoking during 
pregnancy is one of the major causes of Sudden Infant Death 
Syndrome (SIDS), including low birth weight. Some of the 
reports show that  nasal cancer is associated with smoking. 
Madam, India is the world's third largest tobacco 
producing country. Nearly 50 per cent of the tobacco produced 
is consumed in the domestic market annually. In 1992, India 
produced about 767,436 million manufactured cigarettes and 
bidis, accounting for 13.5 per cent of the world's total. Of these, 
about 2,100 million cigarettes were exported. India's earnings 
from tobacco exports totalled at US $ 127.7 million. 
This seems to be the main consideration for India 
clearing a proposal to allow India Tobacco Corporation to triple 
the capacity of its Kidderpore Plant in Calcutta from 4.8 billion 
to 12.25 billion cigarettes. Similarly, the Government has 
allowed cent per cent FDI in India for the U.K. based 
Rothmans of Pall Mall International and to set up a new $ 150 
million plant. 
However, we must not forget that the revenue earned 
from the tobacco industry is far less than the expenditure 
incurred on patients suffering from tobacco-related diseases.

RAJYA   SABHA [24 November. 2000]  
While it is heartening that some States, including the 
National Capita! Territory of Delhi, are conscious of the 
hazards of smoking and have undertaken suitable legislation in 
this regard, their implementation is half-hearted, as indicated in 
a recent Press report. I quote: 
"In a startling revelation, it has come to light that at 
least 25 per cent of the persons challaned or fined for 
violating the provisions of Delhi Prohibition of Smoking 
Act in public transport buses and Government offices 
during the past two years were the ones supposed to 
ensure the enforcement of the same law. The offenders 
include employees who were found smoking within 
Government office premises or in the Delhi Transport 
Corporation buses and those running under the DTC's   
Kilometre Scheme." 
The contention that smoking causes disease is almost 
as old as the use of tobacco itself. One of the first published 
reports on the subject was issued in 1859; it showed that of 68 
patients in a hospital at Montpellier. France, who had cancer of 
the lips, tongue, tonsils or other parts of the mouth, used 
tobacco. 
It is imperative that the society should have healthy 
outlets. Some of the charges levelled against smoking are: 
(a) Smoking becomes an instrument for retract and 
withdrawal from 
society. It invariably rejects the values and life-styles of 
others along with at times being a visible means of 
dissent. Above all, it represents a new pleasure ethic 
that tries to break down the old work ethic. 
(b) Smokers seem to have a low level of tolerance in terms 
of anxiety and frustration. They are always eager to use 
props whenever they feel insecure. 
(c) It is said that smokers suffer from weak e;)o and super 
ego. They are unable to resolve their emotional and 
neurotic conflicts underlying in their psyche. 
We must try and combat the menace of smoking 
urgently. There is no time to lose. A firm Central legislation is 
the only remedy. A beginning can be made with prevention of 
smoking tobacco, in any form, at places of work and in public 
transport vehicles immediately 
The question was proposed.
